card.hook: Step onto the bridge sidewalk, look across the harbour, and there they are: the Atlantis towers rising behind the water, with the bridge's road curving right toward them. It's the classic Atlantis skyline view, and it's free.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pedestrian sidewalk of Sir Sidney Poitier Bridge, on the Paradise Island side. Face across the harbour: the resort lies to the north, with the Nassau skyline around it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the resort, the harbour and the bridge all fit in one frame. Try 0.5x for more bridge and skyline, then 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to make the towers look bigger against the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the towers on an upper intersection with water filling the bottom third, then tap the towers and slide the brightness down a little so the sky and towers keep their detail.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the towers and water than harsh midday sun. If you stay for dusk, use night mode and hold your phone very still against the railing or your body.
card.selfie_here: Try Marina Village at Atlantis, on the street near the water with the docked yachts in front and the towers behind. Use the front camera (or 0.5x if your phone has it on the front) and keep the towers over your shoulder. Marina Village is inside the resort complex, so check access before you go.
card.ask_someone: On the approach to the Paradise Island Bridge, hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to frame the resort skyline with you in the picture.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep to the sidewalk, because this is the main road bridge to the island and traffic is close by. The resort itself is private, so don't plan on photographing from inside it.
card.challenge: Make the bridge's road span lead the eye straight to the towers, and see if you can get the water to fill exactly the bottom third.
card.good_to_know: Atlantis covers 154 acres and has five hotels, including the Royal, Coral, Cove and Reef Towers. The Royal Towers opened on 11 December 1998, when the site was rebranded as Atlantis. There's also a waterpark, a big open-air marine habitat and a marina for yachts.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pedestrian sidewalk of Sir Sidney Poitier Bridge, on the Paradise Island side. Face across the harbour: the resort lies to the north, with the Nassau skyline around it.

selfie_research.safety: Lock up cash, cards, laptops, phones and small electronics, since one forum post says these are the items usually stolen at the resort.
selfie_research.notes: The sources are blogs, forums and photo-spot guides, some of them old (a 2014 blog, a 2019 post and a 16-year-old forum thread), so check current access. Atlantis is a private resort: Cove Beach and the resort grounds may require a hotel stay, day pass, or approved access, and some pages say professional photography may need confirmation. No page I found gives a precise pin for the bridge approach or the exact palm tree, and no page stated rules on selfie sticks or tripods. The Atlantis resort's own photographers were mentioned as stationed around the property and on Cove Beach at sunset, but they are staff, not passers-by, so I did not use them as the ask-someone spot.

card.hook: Paradise Island used to be called Hog Island, which is not quite the postcard name you'd expect from those glossy resort towers. From high up on Bennet's Hill, the whole layered scene of harbour, boats and island is yours.
card.stand_here: Stand on the top landing of Fort Fincastle on Bennet's Hill, the highest point on New Providence. Face north-east and Paradise Island is spread out below you across Nassau Harbour.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole harbour in. Then try 2x or 5x to pick the resort towers out from the greenery (higher zooms depend on your phone). Use 0.5x only if you want lots of sky and foreground.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on your gridlines and sit the horizon on one line so it stays level, with the harbour water filling the bottom half and the island in the upper third.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day. A morning or later in the afternoon is worth trying for the harbour colours.
card.selfie_here: Head to the pedestrian walkway on the Sir Sidney Poitier Bridge, on the sidewalk of the western harbour bridge to Paradise Island. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the Atlantis towers sit across the water over your shoulder. Or try near the gazebo in the Versailles Gardens at the Cloisters on Paradise Island Drive, where the medieval marble cloister makes a distinctive backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Stand at the Paradise Island end of the bridge approach with the Atlantis skyline behind you, and ask a passer-by to take the shot facing you.
card.rules_and_safety: Fort Fincastle is a paid spot and was listed as temporarily closed during renovation of the nearby Water Tower, so check before you go. If you head to Cabbage Beach, waves and currents can be strong, so swim near lifeguards.
card.challenge: Can you get the horizon dead level and the island sitting neatly in the top third, with not a single tilted tower?
card.good_to_know: The island was called Hog Island until 1962, when developer Huntington Hartford renamed it. It covers about 277 hectares and is best known today for the Atlantis resort. Two bridges link it to New Providence: the first was built in 1966 and the second in the late 1990s.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the top landing of Fort Fincastle on Bennet's Hill, the highest point on New Providence. Face north-east and Paradise Island is spread out below you across Nassau Harbour.

card.hook: Picture a pale strip of sand, calm shallow water and hardly anything else in your way. That's Goodman's Bay Park, and it's a very easy place to take a good photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Goodman's Bay Park, on the shoreline stretch along Cable Beach. The middle of Cable Beach is about 2.4 km to the west, so face west and shoot along the shoreline.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the full sweep of sand, water and sky. Switch to 1x for a more natural look. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a distant hotel or someone walking at the water's edge.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sand, then slide the brightness a little darker so the bright sand doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Go on a weekday if you can, when the park is calmer and there are fewer people in your frame. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday.
card.selfie_here: Head to the quieter stretch near the shoreline in Goodman's Bay Park and stand with the sea at your back. Use the front camera, and if your phone has a 0.5x option, try it to fit more water and sky in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Expect vendors and jet skis on the busier sections of the beach, and parking near Goodman's Bay can be tight.
card.challenge: Put the horizon on a gridline, keep a strip of sand in the foreground, and see if you can get it perfectly level on the first try.
card.good_to_know: Cable Beach runs for about two and a half miles along the northern coast of New Providence. The name is said to come from an 1892 submarine telegraph cable linking Jupiter, Florida to Goodman's Bay. Tourism here goes back to the 1940s, and by the 1950s it was a centre for hotel building, later promoted as the "Bahamian Riviera".
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Goodman's Bay Park, on the shoreline stretch along Cable Beach. The middle of Cable Beach is about 2.4 km to the west, so face west and shoot along the shoreline.

card.hook: Turquoise water, painted beach bars and a harbour lighthouse, all in one short stroll. Junkanoo Beach is lively rather than peaceful, and that's exactly what makes the photos fun.
card.stand_here: Walk to the end of the beach that faces the harbour lighthouse. The phone icon on the map marks the spot, so face the lighthouse and let the water and sky fill the frame. The exact point is approximate, so shuffle a few steps along the sand until the lighthouse has clear space around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the lighthouse with water and sky around it. Then turn round and switch to zoom 0.5x to fit the shoreline, the people and the bright water into one frame. If your phone has zoom 2x or 5x, use it to pull the lighthouse closer and leave the beach clutter out.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the lighthouse, then drag the brightness down a little so the sky keeps its colour, and turn on gridlines to put the lighthouse on a vertical line.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or on a day with no cruise ships in port, when the beach is easier to shoot. Later in the day, sunset light can add colour to the lighthouse view.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the sand in front of the brightly painted beach shacks with the sea behind you, so all that colour ends up in the frame. Use the front camera, switch to zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a little lower and further out so more of the scene fits behind your shoulder. For a second go, try the concrete seawall at the edge of the beach with the water behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Some visitors mention pushy vendors on the beach, so keep your phone and bags close when you hand your phone to a stranger. This looks like an open beach, but check the official site before you go for any access or facility rules.
card.challenge: Get the lighthouse on a gridline with a dead-level horizon, then spin round and catch the whole beach buzz in one 0.5x shot.
card.good_to_know: Junkanoo Beach has the harbour on one side and beach bars and chair rentals along the back. Crowds are heaviest when cruise ships are in port. The Tiki Bikini Hut, a colourful bar against clear blue water with cruise ships docked nearby, makes a third photo option.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the end of the beach that faces the harbour lighthouse. The phone icon on the map marks the spot, so face the lighthouse and let the water and sky fill the frame. The exact point is approximate, so shuffle a few steps along the sand until the lighthouse has clear space around it.

card.hook: Count the steps and you'll get about 65, but everyone in Nassau calls this the 66 steps. Stand in the middle of the flight, between the rock walls and the dripping ferns, and you'll see why it's worth the climb.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Queen's Staircase itself, about halfway up the flight, at the phone icon on the map. Turn around and face back down the steps towards the street.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the view down the corridor. Then try 0.5x to squeeze the walls, greenery and steps all into the frame, since the space is tight.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the centre of the steps up with the middle of the frame, and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Go early morning or late afternoon, when it's quieter and the cruise-ship crowds are smaller. On cruise-ship days it can get very busy.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie, go to the waterfall pool at the foot of the steps, where the spray keeps the ferns green. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x and hold your phone a little low so the greenery and the stairs fit behind you. You can also pause on one of the flat landings partway up and do the same with the stairway around you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the foot of the steps near the waterfall pool and shoot up, while you pose a few steps up so the whole stairway and the greenery fit in.
card.rules_and_safety: The limestone steps are worn smooth and get slippery when wet, especially the lower third near the waterfall spray, so wear shoes with grip. They're steep and there's no easier route, so take your time and watch your footing while you hold your phone. Fort Fincastle at the top is a separate site, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot from halfway up and one from the base with the cascade and ferns in front, then pick your favourite and see if you can guess which one wins.
card.good_to_know: About 600 enslaved workers carved the staircase straight into solid limestone between 1793 and 1794. It links Fort Fincastle with the town below and was named for Queen Victoria in the 19th century. The whole flight rises about 31 metres (102 feet).
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Queen's Staircase itself, about halfway up the flight, at the phone icon on the map. Turn around and face back down the steps towards the street.

card.hook: Picture a sandy path squeezed between two resorts, then suddenly a wide sweep of white sand and turquoise sea opens up below you. That's the Cabbage Beach reveal, and it's about as easy as holiday photos get.
card.stand_here: Stand at the top of the public access path on Casino Drive, between the resort properties, and check the exact spot on the map because it's easy to miss. Face the sea and shoot down onto the shoreline.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in all the sand, sea and sky. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x to pick out the breakwater or a faraway swimmer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the sea, then drag the brightness down a little so the sand stays sandy instead of turning plain white.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is usually softer. Midday sun bleaches the sand, so it's worth skipping.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the public access path just to the right of the Riu Palace, where the path first opens onto the sand, with the sea behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x if your phone has it, so the sand and turquoise water fit over your shoulder. For something different, walk to the far end of the beach to the rock formation, which one local photographer's guide calls one of the best photo places in Nassau. Check the map to find it.
card.rules_and_safety: No lifeguards are on duty at Cabbage Beach and rip currents can be very strong, so be careful in the water. At the Thunderball Breakwater the ground is rough and the currents are strong, so don't swim there. Some beach areas are reserved for hotel guests, and reaching the breakwater may involve Atlantis, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Put the horizon on a gridline and get a loungers-and-umbrellas-free shot. Yes, it's harder than it sounds.
card.good_to_know: Cabbage Beach is a long, wide stretch of white sand beside the Atlantic. Vendors rent out chairs, so you may need to frame around loungers and umbrellas, or walk along the sand to find quieter stretches. Salt haze makes pictures look soft, so wipe your phone's camera before you shoot.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the top of the public access path on Casino Drive, between the resort properties, and check the exact spot on the map because it's easy to miss. Face the sea and shoot down onto the shoreline.

card.hook: Nobody tells you the best bit of Fort Fincastle is the climb. A long flight of limestone steps, tropical greenery down one side, and a fort waiting at the top like a reward.
card.stand_here: Stand at the foot of the Queen's Staircase and look up the full flight. The fort is to the north-west, at the top.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole run of steps. If it feels cramped, try 0.5x. Zoom 2x squeezes the steps together and makes the fort look closer.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and run the steps along a diagonal or the centre line, holding your phone low and level so they stay straight.
card.best_time: Go in the morning. One guide says the light is softer and the crowds are thinner then. The steps are also shaded, which helps on a bright day.
card.selfie_here: Climb to the lower steps of the Queen's Staircase beside the waterfall and turn to face back down the stairs, so the fort is above you. Use the front camera, and if it has a 0.5x button, try it to fit in the rock walls and greenery. If you go up into the fort, the upper platform by the cannons is another good spot, and with the right angle a cannon looks aimed at the cruise ships.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a few steps below you on the staircase and shoot up toward the fort while you pose on the steps (the stairs start from Elizabeth Avenue).
card.rules_and_safety: Some steps on the Queen's Staircase are uneven and at different distances apart, so watch your feet while you climb. The staircase is free, but the fort itself is ticketed and may be closed at times, so check the official site before you go. Photography is generally allowed inside and around the fort.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the steps run dead straight up to the fort, then one where you're clearly out of breath from the climb. Keep whichever is more honest.
card.good_to_know: Lord Dunmore had Fort Fincastle built in 1793 to protect Nassau from pirates, and named it after his second title, Viscount Fincastle. The fort is shaped like a paddle steamer. It also worked as a lighthouse until September 1817, when the lighthouse on Paradise Island took over.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the foot of the Queen's Staircase and look up the full flight. The fort is to the north-west, at the top.

card.hook: Most people dive straight into the Straw Market to hunt for bargains and walk right past the front. Stop for a second, because the facade is prettier than you'd expect.
card.stand_here: Stand near the corner of Bay Street and Market Street, about 56 m south-east of the market, and look north-west towards the Bay Street frontage. The street corner frames the building nicely.
card.zoom: Start at 1x and fit the whole facade in, entrance included. If the pavement is too narrow, try 0.5x but keep the building upright so the edges don't lean. Use 2x for a tighter shot of the entrance and signage.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines so the building's edges stay straight, and let a few people walk past the entrance to give the picture some life.
card.best_time: It's busiest from roughly 10:00 to 15:00 on days when cruise ships are in port, so go earlier or later for cleaner pictures. If you can, check which days ships are due.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the Bay Street sidewalk in front of the Straw Market facade (Bay St & Market St corner), with the market's front entrance and facade behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the building over your shoulder. For a different look, take one inside, in an aisle beside a stall of handwoven bags and hats, with the stock filling the frame behind you (ask first, and a morning visit is calmer).
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sidewalk at the corner of Bay Street and Market Street with the market's front in view, so the whole building fits in your photo.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask vendors before taking close-ups of them or their goods. One guide says many will then show you how they weave. If the pavement is crowded, step back to the kerb edge, but take care with traffic.
card.challenge: Get the whole facade in with the entrance, straight edges on the gridlines, and one stranger walking through at just the right moment.
card.good_to_know: The Straw Market is a market building on Bay Street in central Nassau. The pink and white colonial-style buildings along Bay Street make a soft, colourful backdrop, so squeeze some into your shot for a sense of place. It's worth checking on the day whether the market looks best from outside or inside.

card.hook: Picture a proper stone fort with an arched gate, a drawbridge and a row of cannons that never had to fight anyone. Fort Charlotte has had a very quiet life, and it makes a great first photo.
card.stand_here: Stand right where the phone icon sits, in front of the arched main gate at Fort Charlotte. Face the gate so the drawbridge and cannons are in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the arch, towers, drawbridge and cannons all fit in one shot. Switch to 1x for a straighter, more natural look, then try 2x-5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for close-ups of the cannons, stone blocks and flag.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the arch up with the centre, and keep a cannon or a bit of drawbridge in the foreground for depth.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light brings out the texture of the stone.
card.selfie_here: Head to the northeast corner of the upper level, where the cannons point toward the water. Use your front camera (tap 0.5x if yours has it) with the cannons and harbour behind you, and a cruise ship may sneak into the background. The dry moat floor also works, with the tall stone walls rising behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the approach in front of the arched gate and towers, far enough back to fit the whole facade, cannons and flag, while you pose at the gate.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is permitted throughout the fort, but check the rules before flying a drone. Wear shoes with grip, as the underground passages have ducking spaces and uneven stone floors.
card.challenge: Find a cannon pointing at the water and line it up with a cruise ship in the distance, then see if you can get both in one shot.
card.good_to_know: Lord Dunmore, the colonial governor, built this British fort in the late 18th century, after the American Revolutionary War. It was never used in battle. The site is roughly 200 metres across, so there's plenty to explore.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right where the phone icon sits, in front of the arched main gate at Fort Charlotte. Face the gate so the drawbridge and cannons are in the frame.

card.hook: Most people come to Arawak Cay for the food, but the island itself is the surprise: people made it, out of mud dredged from Nassau Harbour. Walk out to the water's edge at sunset and you'll see why it's worth a camera-roll detour.
card.stand_here: Stand on Arawak Cay Promenade, on the western part of the cay, and face out over the harbour and the nearby islands. Keep a bit of the path or railing at the bottom of your shot to give it depth.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the whole sweep of harbour and sky, then try 1x for a more natural look at the water. Tap 2x up to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out a single island or boat against the sunset colours.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, tap the brightest part of the sky, then slide it a little darker so the oranges and pinks don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go at sunset, when the sky can turn orange and pink. Weekends and after dark are busiest, so pick a quieter time if you want fewer people in your shots.
card.selfie_here: Head to the beach strip in front of the painted vendor stalls and stand on the sand, with the conch shell pile in front of you and the coloured stalls behind. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more stalls in, and keep them over your shoulder. The 'Fish Fry Street' sign on West Bay Street is another popular photo spot, though we can't tell you exactly where it sits along the row.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the West Bay Street roadside facing the row of stalls while you stand in front of them, so the whole colourful strip is behind you (check the angle on the spot).
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working port area, so check the official site before you go for any restrictions. After dark, take a taxi back to downtown rather than walking, as the Nassau Guardian guide suggests.
card.challenge: Find the conch shell pile and get one photo where the shells, the painted stalls and the harbour all squeeze into the same frame. Bonus points if you look hungry.
card.good_to_know: Arawak Cay is a 100-acre island, built in 1969 from material dredged out of Nassau Harbour. Shipping began here in the 1980s, and Nassau Container Port was added in 2011. Today most visitors come for the local eateries along West Bay Street, which is why it's also known as the Fish Fry.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Arawak Cay Promenade, on the western part of the cay, and face out over the harbour and the nearby islands. Keep a bit of the path or railing at the bottom of your shot to give it depth.

card.hook: Picture a little limestone fort sitting right at the edge of the sand, with just four cannon left to guard it. Fort Montagu is small, so it fits neatly in your phone frame.
card.stand_here: Stand on Montagu Beach, on the sand in front of the fort, and turn around to look back at the walls. They rise above the beach, with the harbour and resort buildings across the water behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the sand, the walls and the sky all in one shot. Switch to 1x for a cleaner view of the fort, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the stonework or boats on the harbour.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, put the horizon on a line so it stays level, and tap the stone wall so it looks crisp.
card.best_time: Afternoon is likely to suit this view, because the sun should be behind you and light up the walls. Early morning may put the fort against the light.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at 0.5x and stand beside one of the old cannons along the fort's outer edge, so the limestone is over your shoulder. You can also try the rocks beside the walkway closest to the water. One reviewer liked it as a photo spot, but check the fort actually fits behind you when you get there.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sand at the eastern end of Montagu Beach, facing the fort, while you pose in front of the walls so the fort fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The beach is open to everyone, but the fort grounds and any tour inside may have their own access rules, so check the official site before you go. Seaweed has been reported on the beach on some visits, so look at the sand before you frame your shot.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of sand, walls and sky, then walk closer and fill the whole frame with stonework. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: Work on Fort Montagu began in 1741 under the military engineer Peter Henry Bruce, to guard the island against Spanish attack, and it was finished the following year. Later, in the American Revolutionary War, American forces took it before moving on to Nassau itself.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Montagu Beach, on the sand in front of the fort, and turn around to look back at the walls. They rise above the beach, with the harbour and resort buildings across the water behind them.

card.hook: Picture a line of pink flamingos marching straight toward you, with a keeper strolling alongside like a very relaxed parade marshal. That's the Ardastra Gardens show, and it's the best photo moment here.
card.stand_here: Stand inside the garden in the flamingo arena seating area, where you get an open view of the birds walking up to the crowd. Face the flamingos with the sun behind or beside you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for groups of birds and wider garden scenes. Go to 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for a single flamingo, so you can stay back and still fill the frame. Save 0.5x for broad planted areas and paths, because it makes far-off animals look tiny.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the nearest bird's head, then drag the brightness slider down a touch so the pink and orange feathers stay rich instead of washed out.
card.best_time: Morning or later in the afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows than midday. Check the official site for visiting times before you go.
card.selfie_here: Head into the flamingo arena at the end of the show, when visitors can stand with the flamingos, and use the front camera with a bird beside you. For something leafier, try the small footbridge on the narrow path north toward the Secret Garden, and use 0.5x on the front camera to fit the flowers in behind you.
card.ask_someone: In the arena during the show, the marching flamingos stop in front of each group of visitors, so hand your phone to a neighbour and ask them to shoot you with the birds in front of you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos for personal use are generally fine, but follow any signs about flash or restricted areas. Keep a respectful distance and don't disturb the animals for a photo.
card.challenge: Wait for the moment a flamingo lifts its head or stretches its wings, then see if you can catch it, with a clean line of birds and green planting behind.
card.good_to_know: Ardastra Gardens opened in 1937, the work of Jamaican horticulturist Hedley Vivian Edwards. The name comes from the Latin Ardua astrum, meaning "Striving for the stars". The flamingos arrived in the 1950s, brought in by the Bahamian government to breed because they had become rare locally. Today the zoo holds about 200 animals.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand inside the garden in the flamingo arena seating area, where you get an open view of the birds walking up to the crowd. Face the flamingos with the sun behind or beside you.

card.hook: Picture a marble Queen Victoria standing calm in the middle of Nassau's souvenir-stall bustle, with pink-and-white government buildings glowing behind her. That's your photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Parliament Square, in front of the Senate, a short walk west of the cruise port. Face the pink colonial buildings and the Queen Victoria statue.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the statue with the pink buildings behind it. Try 0.5x to squeeze in more street and building fronts, or 2x to pick out details without walking closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the statue, then drag the slider down so it's a little darker and the white stone and pale walls keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go earlier in the day, or when fewer cruise ships are in port, for a calmer street. Pick a time when the sun isn't directly behind the statue.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Straw Market's pastel front on the pavement at the Bay Street and Market Street corner, with the street behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x to fit more of that colourful backdrop in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Frederick Street corner and frame you with Bay Street stretching away behind you (it's worth a quick check on arrival that the view works).
card.rules_and_safety: There are no general photo restrictions on Bay Street itself, but individual shops may have their own policies. Stay aware of your surroundings in crowds, and ask before photographing people. If you plan to go inside any government buildings, check the official site first.
card.challenge: Get the statue on one third of the frame with the pink buildings behind it, and not a single stray bag or sign in the corners. Take a few frames, since people keep walking through.
card.good_to_know: Bay Street is a centre for politics, business, culture and tourism in The Bahamas. When Nassau was founded, somewhere between 1648 and 1666, the street was known as "The Strand". Today it's lined with souvenir stalls and shopfronts, so your photo can show old and new together.

card.hook: You can't miss it: a bright conch-pink house with white trim, sitting on a hill above downtown Nassau and looking very pleased with itself. It looks cheerful on a phone screen, too.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Duke Street and George Street, on the uphill approach, and face south towards the front of the house. From here you can fit the pink-and-white front, the columns, the circular drive and the statue into one picture without going through any gate.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole front, the columns and the Columbus statue in one shot. If the pavement is too narrow to step back, switch to 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the pediment, columns and roof.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the columns upright, so the front looks straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Morning and late afternoon light suit the building best, according to a photography guide.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and stand by the Columbus statue at the front of the house, with the pink facade behind you, if you can get close enough. The ceremonial cannons outside the house also make a fun historic prop with the pink wall behind them. Each spot comes from a single guide, so check them when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone on the public Duke Street sidewalk opposite the grounds, where the bright front shows from the street, and pose with the pink house behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working residence, so access to the grounds is limited and can change. Check the official site before you go, and treat the street corner as your safe default. Some paths around the hillside can be steep and uneven, so take care.
card.challenge: Get the pink front, the columns, the circular drive and the statue all in one frame, with the columns dead straight on the gridlines.
card.good_to_know: The house was completed in 1806 on a rise known as Mount Fitzwilliam, and it's often called the country's finest example of Georgian Colonial building. The columned front you see today dates from the 1930s, when the house was remodelled after the hurricane of 1929. The 12-foot Columbus statue was placed in front in 1830. It's a controversial figure, so decide whether you want it in your frame.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Duke Street and George Street, on the uphill approach, and face south towards the front of the house. From here you can fit the pink-and-white front, the columns, the circular drive and the statue into one picture without going through any gate.

card.hook: Pink walls, green palms, blue sky: Nassau has already picked the colour scheme for you. All you have to do is point your phone at it.
card.stand_here: Stand in Parliament Square, in front of the Senate building, with the Queen Victoria statue as your foreground. Face south, with the statue low in the frame and the pink buildings and palms behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the statue and the pink buildings sit together nicely. If the square is crowded, try zoom 0.5x to fit in more of the buildings. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) is good for close-ups of the statue or the rooflines.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the statue on a lower third point, and keep your phone level so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the pink walls look their best. Weekdays and cruise-ship days get busy, so wait for a gap in the crowd or shoot a bit wider and let a few people into the picture.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the Queen Victoria statue in front of the Senate building, with the pink facade behind you. Use the front camera, and try zoom 0.5x if you want the whole pink wall over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across Bay Street from the square, where the three pink buildings and the statue all fit in the frame, while you pose by the statue.
card.rules_and_safety: Stick to the outside: photography is usually not allowed inside the government buildings, and the building may be off-limits to photographers on some days. Watch the traffic on Bay Street when you cross to the spot opposite the square. Construction equipment has sometimes appeared nearby, so check the edges of your frame before you shoot.
card.challenge: Can you get the statue, the pink wall and a palm frond all in one shot without a single stranger in it? Good luck on a cruise day!
card.good_to_know: The Parliament Building is home to the House of Assembly, and it sits on Parliament Square on Bay Street. Loyalist refugees from the newly independent United States built the complex in 1815. Its British colonial style is often compared with American Federal architecture.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Parliament Square, in front of the Senate building, with the Queen Victoria statue as your foreground. Face south, with the statue low in the frame and the pink buildings and palms behind it.

selfie_research.notes: No page mentions selfie sticks or tripods, so no rule is given for them. The selfie spots come from general photo guides, not pages written about selfies, so they are photo spots adapted for selfies. The Royal Victoria Garden detail comes from a generic guide with thin sourcing, so check it on the ground. Sources use both 'Parliament Square' and 'Rawson Square' for the same area. card.hook: Downtown Nassau is busy, and then this solid Gothic kirk with its tower turns up among the streets looking like it has stood there forever. Scottish settlers started the story in 1798, so it has a bit of history to show off.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Prince's Street and Peck's Slope, opposite the Central Bank building, and face the Kirk across Prince's Street so you get the Gothic front and the tower.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x and hold your phone upright to fit the full height of the building. Use 0.5x only if the street is too tight, then zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the doorway, windows and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the church's straight edges up with them so the walls don't lean, then tap the church wall and slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the walls. Midday shadows can be harsh and the sky can look washed out.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt it up a little so the tower sits over your shoulder. Keep the building behind you and smile like you meant to be there.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working church, so be considerate if a service is under way and dress respectfully. Stay on the pavement and keep clear of traffic, and check the official site before you go to see if visitors can go inside.
card.challenge: Take your wide shot first, then move in and get the entrance all by itself, like a movie poster for the Kirk.
card.good_to_know: It began in 1798, when fifty-five Scottish Presbyterian settlers formed the St. Andrew Society. The foundation stone was laid on 7 August 1810, and a session room was added in 1842 for a growing congregation. Inside there are two stained glass windows either side of the communion table.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Prince's Street and Peck's Slope, opposite the Central Bank building, and face the Kirk across Prince's Street so you get the Gothic front and the tower.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the Kirk behind the visitor, or a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph the visitor with the whole building, so both fields are empty. The closest material is generic: an Airial guide says the stained glass windows and exterior architecture are good photo subjects, but it names no place to stand. Locations found but not vetted as photo spots: the Kirk is on Prince's Street at Peck's Slope, opposite Central Bank (trubahamianfoodtours.com, bahamaslocal.com), and the Waymarking entry gives coordinates matching your position. Search coverage was limited, so a local check on the ground or a fresh search of Nassau photo-walk guides may still find a named spot. No page I found states any selfie-stick or tripod rule. The one photography point I found is that Airial advises against photographing during services and says exterior shots may be allowed if you ask first. I left it out of rules because it is not about selfie sticks or tripods and is not a rule the page states as official.

card.hook: Here's a fun trick: the cathedral is only half the picture. The pink government buildings behind it do the heavy lifting, and with a blue sky on top you get three colours in one shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on West Hill Street and face the cathedral, so the pink government buildings sit right behind it. It's an ordinary public street, so you can take your time.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the cathedral and the pink buildings together. Try 0.5x if you want more street and sky, then 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the cathedral against the pink.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the cathedral on one of the vertical lines so it stands straight, then tap the cathedral and drag it a touch darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Mid-morning or early afternoon is the sweet spot for this view.
card.selfie_here: Walk through Gregory's Arch, near the cathedral. The arch frames the building and gives you a shaded backdrop, and late afternoon is best. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the cathedral over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo from West Hill Street, where the cathedral and the pink buildings fit in one shot, while you stand with the cathedral behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside the church may be restricted, so confirm the policy and the opening hours before you go. On West Hill Street, keep an eye out for traffic and other people.
card.challenge: Take two shots: one wide to show the whole scene, and one close on the cathedral alone, then pick your favourite and see if the blue sky made it.
card.good_to_know: Christ Church Cathedral is in central downtown Nassau, with the pink government buildings behind it. Rawson Square, the open plaza in the centre of town, is the other good place to see it from, with everyday street life around it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on West Hill Street and face the cathedral, so the pink government buildings sit right behind it. It's an ordinary public street, so you can take your time.

card.hook: The cathedral sits at the top of a steep street, with a tall steeple poking up into that big tropical sky. Climb the street and you get a postcard, but only if you pick your spot.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of West Street and West Hill Street, where the historic facade and entrance face the street. Face the cathedral so the steeple sits right above the entrance.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the facade and entrance. If the street is too tight to fit the steeple in, tap 0.5x, and try 2x for close-ups of the steeple and entrance details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the entrance up with the centre of the frame, and leave some sky above the steeple.
card.best_time: Morning light is suggested for the outside. If you want the stained glass inside, midday is better.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the sidewalk in front of the entrance on West Hill Street, with the facade behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a bit low so the steeple fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working place of worship, so check the official site for visiting times and photo rules. Inside, personal photos are generally fine, but no flash during services.
card.challenge: Take two shots from a few steps apart: the old facade all on its own, then the old and new cathedrals together. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: This is the mother church of The Bahamas and the first Catholic church in the country. The first Mass was in November 1886, and it became a cathedral in 1960. A newer cathedral was dedicated in 2004, just 17 metres away, and the old building is still in use.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of West Street and West Hill Street, where the historic facade and entrance face the street. Face the cathedral so the steeple sits right above the entrance.

selfie_spots.name: Cathedral facade at the main entrance, West Hill Street
selfie_spots.detail: on the sidewalk in front of the entrance, with the facade behind you
selfie_spots.why: Airial's photo guide names the facade and entrance as the strongest exterior photo subject, and the cathedral sits on West Hill Street.

card.hook: You're on Paradise Island, but the roofless stone arches in front of you look like they were lifted out of a European monastery. That's close to the truth, and it makes a great frame.
card.stand_here: Stand on the cloister steps, right where the phone icon sits, so there's no extra walk once you're in the gardens. Face out towards Nassau Harbour so the arches are in front of you and the water shows through behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x on the steps to squeeze the whole row of arches in, then switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a single arch or a close-up of the columns with the water behind.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines, then tap the stone and nudge it darker if the bright water looks washed out.
card.best_time: Go early morning for fewer people and softer light, or late afternoon for warmer light on the stone. The cloister is popular with wedding and engagement photographers, so it can get busy.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the cloister steps at the top of the terraced lawn, with the arches over your shoulder. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone offers it so more of the stonework fits in. For a second one, head to the lily pad pond at the top of the garden's central walkway, with the bronze statues nearby.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the bottom of the terraced lawn and shoot up the steps, while you stand up by the cloister.
card.rules_and_safety: Access isn't clear. The cloister may be open to everyone or limited to Ocean Club guests, so check on arrival and follow any staff instructions.
card.challenge: Catch the harbour in the gap between two columns, with the nearest arch framing it and nobody walking through.
card.good_to_know: The cloister is said to come from a European Augustinian monastery that was taken apart, shipped over and rebuilt stone by stone here. Its age is given as anything from the 12th to the 14th century. One side looks out to Nassau Harbour and the other to the Ocean Club resort.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the cloister steps, right where the phone icon sits, so there's no extra walk once you're in the gardens. Face out towards Nassau Harbour so the arches are in front of you and the water shows through behind them.

selfie_research.notes: Position 25.08028, -77.31000 is on Paradise Island, not the Nassau mainland. Access is doubtful: several pages say the gardens sit within the Four Seasons Ocean Club grounds and that guards may turn non-guests away, while others describe them as a free public park, so check on arrival. Sources disagree on the cloister's date (12th vs 14th century). The lily-pad pond spot and the passer-by spot are inferred from layout descriptions, not from pages giving photo instructions, so the exact framing is unconfirmed. No page I found states selfie stick or tripod rules for this site; the Magic Ways pages cover the Château de Versailles in France and were excluded.
